verdict.rationale: The canon places restrictive wording ("I do not permit a woman to teach or to exercise/usurp authority over a man" (didaskein de gynaiki ouk epitrepo oude authentein andros) in 1 Timothy 2:12, and "let them keep silent" (sigatosan) and "let them be in submission" (hypotassesthosan) in 1 Corinthians 14:34) beside the male-marked office qualifications ("husband of one wife" (mias gynaikos andra) in 1 Timothy 3:2 and Titus 1:6) and over against texts of mutual standing and female ministry (Galatians 3:28, Phoebe called a servant/minister (Phoibe diakonos) in Romans 16:1, and the name "Junia" (Iounian) in Romans 16:7). The verdict turns on word-forms (lemmas, the dictionary headword forms) whose sense the words do not settle. A direct query confirms "to exercise authority" or "to domineer" (authenteo, G0831) is a hapax (a word that occurs only once in the entire Bible) at 1 Timothy 2:12, and the lexicon itself records both a neutral sense, to have full power or authority over, and a pejorative sense, to domineer, with no second canonical use to fix which is meant. The present-tense form "I do not permit" (epitrepo, G2010, an ongoing simple statement of fact) is the same verb used elsewhere for granting permission to speak in a particular setting, and "to keep silent" (sigao, G4601) appears three times in 1 Corinthians 14 (verses 28, 30, 34), the first two governing specific disorders, so the scope of the women command is contestable between an absolute prohibition and a setting-bound one. The office noun "overseer" (episkopos) is grammatically masculine and the "husband of one wife" (mias gynaikos andra) clause presupposes a married male on its surface, yet that clause can be read as a fidelity standard, and the 1 Corinthians 14:34-35 unit carries a known transposition (a passage moved to a different location in some manuscripts) the ingested apparatus cannot adjudicate. Because the same word-forms (lemmas) yield more than one grammatically defensible reading, the lexical pattern is contested rather than decisive.

scripture.force: "I do not permit a woman to teach or to exercise/usurp authority over a man, but to be in quietness" (didaskein de gynaiki ouk epitrepo oude authentein andros, all einai en hesychia). Two infinitives (verbal forms equivalent to English "to-" forms), "to teach" (didaskein) and "to exercise/usurp authority" (authentein, the verb in question), are joined by the Greek conjunction "nor" (oude). A direct query confirms "to exercise authority" or "to domineer" (authenteo) occurs nowhere else in the canon, so it is a hapax (a word that occurs only once in the entire Bible), and the lexicon records it with both a neutral sense, to have full power or authority over, and a pejorative sense, to domineer, leaving the canon with no second use to fix the force. "I do not permit" (epitrepo) is a first person present (an ongoing, simple statement of fact), and the same verb is used elsewhere for granting permission to speak in a particular instance, so it is debated whether it states a standing rule or a directive in a situation. The two infinitives ("to teach" (didaskein) and "to exercise authority" (authentein)) can be read as two separate prohibitions or as one composite idea, to teach in a domineering manner, and the morphology (the word-form analysis) does not decide between them.

"For Adam was formed first, then Eve" (Adam gar protos eplasthe, eita Eua). The Greek word "for" (gar) introduces a ground for the preceding directive, and the appeal to the order of formation pulls the prohibition toward a trans-cultural basis rather than a purely local one. A query confirms both "Adam" (Adam) and "Eve" (Eua) are present in the verse. Whether the order-of-formation argument grounds a permanent office restriction or supports a contextual correction is not fixed by the conjunction alone, since "for" (gar) marks explanation without specifying the scope of what it explains.

"The overseer must be above reproach, the husband of one wife" (dei oun ton episkopon anepilempton einai, mias gynaikos andra). A query confirms "overseer" (episkopos) occurs seven times in the canon and is grammatically masculine here, and the qualification "husband of one wife" (mias gynaikos andra), literally a one-woman man, presupposes a male officeholder in its plain construction. Yet the clause can be read as a character standard for marital fidelity rather than a bare sex requirement, and grammatical masculine gender for an office term does not by itself exclude a female referent, since masculine forms serve as the default for mixed or generic reference in Greek.

"If anyone is above reproach, the husband of one wife" (ei tis estin anenklethos, mias gynaikos aner), set in the context of appointing "elders" (presbyterous) in every town. The same "husband of one wife" (mias gynaikos aner) formula recurs, again presupposing a married male in its surface sense. The opening word "anyone" (tis) is the indefinite pronoun and is not itself sex-marked, so the restriction to men rests on the "husband of one wife" (gynaikos aner) phrase rather than on "anyone" (tis), and that phrase is read by some as a fidelity qualification rather than a sex bar.

"The women are to keep silent in the assemblies" (hai gynaikes en tais ekklesiais sigatosan), "for they are not permitted to speak, but to be in submission" (ou gar epitrepetai autais lalein, alla hypotassesthosan). A query confirms "to keep silent" (sigao) appears three times in this one chapter, at verses 28, 30, and 34, where a tongue-speaker is to "keep silent" (sigato) if there is no interpreter and a prophet is to "keep silent" (sigato) when another receives a revelation. The proximity of three "keep silent" (sigao) commands, each governing a specific disorder, makes the scope of the women command contestable between an absolute prohibition and a setting-bound regulation of disruptive speech.

"There is no male and female" (ouk eni arsen kai thely), "for you are all one in Christ Jesus" (pantes gar hymeis heis este en Christo Iesou). A query confirms the two sex nouns "male" (arsen) and "female" (thely) are both present, joined to "there is" (eni) and "one" (heis). Whether this negation of the male-and-female distinction speaks only to justification (being declared righteous) and inheritance, the immediate argument about heirship and being Abraham's seed, or extends to ministry roles is not settled by the lexemes (the dictionary word-forms), since the context is sonship rather than church office, yet the comprehensiveness of "all one" (pantes heis) pulls against any sex-based exclusion.

"I commend to you Phoebe our sister, who is a servant/minister of the church" (synistemi de hymin Phoiben ten adelphen hemon, ousan diakonon tes ekklesias). A query confirms the noun "servant/minister" (diakonos) is applied to the named woman Phoebe in connection with a specific congregation, and that "servant/minister" (diakonos) occurs in twenty-eight verses ranging from general servant to a recognized function. Because the term spans that range across the canon, it complicates a blanket exclusion of women from recognized service, though it does not by itself establish that Phoebe held the overseeing or teaching office named in the qualification lists.

"Greet Andronicus and Junia" (aspasasthe Andronikon kai Iounian), "who are notable among/to the apostles" (hoitines eisin episemoi en tois apostolois). A query shows the lexical store records the accusative (the direct-object grammatical form) name "Junia" (Iounian) under one Strong number with both a feminine lemma form, "Junia" (Iounia), and a masculine lemma form, "Junias" (Iounias), so the sex of the person is itself a lexical open question. The verse also contains "notable" (episemos) and "apostle" (apostolos). The phrase "among/to the apostles" (en tois apostolois) can mean among the apostles, marking the pair as apostles, or well known to the apostles, marking them as esteemed by the apostles. If "Junia" (Iounia) is feminine and the inclusive sense holds, a woman is numbered among a class of "apostles" (apostoloi), which complicates a strict office restriction.

complicating_texts.resolution: The phrase "there is no male and female" (ouk eni arsen kai thely) negates the sex distinction within standing in Christ and complicates any sex-based office bar. It is addressed by observing that the surrounding argument concerns justification (being declared righteous), sonship, and being Abraham's seed and heirs, not the appointment of overseers, so the lexemes (the dictionary word-forms) establish equal standing without by themselves extending to or excluding office. A query confirms both sex nouns "male" (arsen) and "female" (thely) are present. The text is genuinely two-edged, which contributes to the disputed verdict rather than resolving it.

Phoebe is called a "servant/minister" (diakonos) of the church at Cenchreae, applying a ministry term to a named woman and complicating a blanket exclusion. A query confirms "servant/minister" (diakonos) here and shows the noun ranges across twenty-eight verses from general servant to a designated function, so the title does not by itself prove she held the overseeing or teaching office that the qualification lists describe. The term pulls toward female ministry without settling whether the disputed office was open to women.

Two intertwined lexical questions remain unresolved on the queried data. The store records the accusative (the direct-object grammatical form) "Junia" (Iounian) under one Strong number with both a feminine lemma, "Junia" (Iounia), and a masculine lemma, "Junias" (Iounias), so the sex of the person is genuinely open in the lexical layer, and the prepositional phrase "among/to the apostles" (en tois apostolois) is ambiguous between inclusive among the apostles and comparative well known to the apostles. The ingested data carries the variant name forms but no accentual (relating to Greek accent marks) or contextual datum that closes either question, so it is left unaddressed and flagged as a complicating text the lexical store could not resolve.

The silence command carries a known transposition (a passage moved to a different location in some manuscripts) in the manuscript tradition, where some witnesses place verses 34-35 after verse 40. A direct query of the variant store shows it holds variant units for 3 John only, so this passage falls outside the ingested apparatus (the critical edition of New Testament textual variants) and the location and originality question cannot be examined here. Because the placement bears on how absolutely the command should be read, the matter is left unresolved and flagged, and it is part of why the verdict is recorded as variant-sensitive.

variants.note: A direct query of the ingested variant store confirms VariantUnit data is present for 3 John only, so no apparatus layer (the critical edition of New Testament textual variants) covers 1 Corinthians 14 or 1 Timothy 2. The cited 1 Corinthians 14:34-35 unit is well known to carry a transposition (a passage moved to a different location in some manuscripts) in part of the tradition, where the verses appear after verse 40, and the originality and placement of the silence command bear directly on how absolutely it should be read, so the verdict is marked variant-sensitive. These books fall outside the published CBGM scope (the Coherence-Based Genealogical Method used in modern critical editions), which covers 3 John, so the status is recorded as ecm-shadow (meaning the critical edition has not yet been published for these books).

competing_lens_verdicts.rationale: Reads "I do not permit" (ouk epitrepo) in 1 Timothy 2:12 as a standing rule expressed in the present tense (an ongoing, simple statement of fact), takes the two infinitives "to teach" (didaskein) and "to exercise authority" (authentein) as distinct prohibited acts, teaching and exercising authority, and reads the hapax (a word that occurs only once in the entire Bible) "to exercise authority" (authenteo) in its neutral lexicon sense of holding authority over. It grounds the rule trans-culturally on the creation-order "for" (gar) of 1 Timothy 2:13, Adam formed first, and treats the male-marked "husband of one wife" (mias gynaikos andra) of 1 Timothy 3:2 and Titus 1:6, together with the masculine "overseer" (episkopos), as defining a male officeholder. It reads Galatians 3:28 as equal standing in Christ rather than role, and reads Phoebe's title "servant/minister" (diakonos) and the Romans 16:7 phrase as not establishing the overseeing or teaching office for women, taking "among/to the apostles" (en tois apostolois) as well known to the apostles.

Reads the hapax (a word that occurs only once in the entire Bible) "to exercise authority" (authenteo) in its pejorative lexicon sense, to domineer or usurp, so the prohibition targets domineering rather than ordinary authority, and notes there is no second canonical use to settle the sense. It takes the present-tense "I do not permit" (epitrepo, an ongoing, simple statement of fact) and the situational vocabulary as addressing a particular disorder, and reads the 1 Corinthians 14:34 "keep silent" (sigao) alongside the chapter's two other situational silencings in verses 28 and 30. It takes "husband of one wife" (mias gynaikos andra) as a fidelity qualification rather than a sex bar, reads Galatians 3:28 as comprehensive of male and female, and takes Phoebe "servant/minister" (diakonos) and a feminine Junia counted among the apostles as evidence that recognized ministry, including authoritative roles, was open to women.

Reads the restrictive texts as one point within a trajectory whose direction, traced from the equal-standing language of Galatians 3:28 and the female ministry references, points beyond the first-century application, so that the lexemes (the dictionary word-forms) describe an apostolic instruction whose permanence is itself the contested question rather than a datum the words settle. On this reading the vocabulary fixes what was said but not how far it reaches in time.

hermeneutics.notes: All three lenses operate on the same anchor lemmas (the dictionary headword forms) and reach different conclusions by assigning the hapax (a word that occurs only once in the entire Bible) "to exercise authority" (authenteo) either its neutral or its pejorative lexicon sense, by reading the present-tense "I do not permit" (epitrepo) and "to keep silent" (sigao) as either standing or situational, by construing the grammatical masculine of the office nouns and the "husband of one wife" (mias gynaikos andra) clause as either sex-restrictive or character-descriptive, and by deciding the referential reach of Galatians 3:28 and the sex and standing of Junia. The disagreement is over the sense and scope of contested lexemes (dictionary word-forms), not over agreed morphology (word-form analysis), which is why the lexical pattern is contested rather than decisive. Both lens senses for "to exercise authority" (authenteo) are attested in the queried lexicon, so neither reading can be excluded on lexical grounds alone.

stem_audit.neutralized_form: Determine whether the canonical lexical pattern reserves the overseeing and teaching office to qualified men, examining the restrictive wording of 1 Timothy 2:12 and 1 Corinthians 14:34, the male-marked office qualifications of 1 Timothy 3:2 and Titus 1:6, and the texts of mutual standing and female ministry such as Galatians 3:28, Romans 16:1, and Romans 16:7, without presupposing which set of texts controls.
stem_audit.notes: The stem (the question as originally phrased) frames the proposition as a denial that women are to hold the eldership or teaching-pastor office over mixed adult assemblies, which already encodes a particular harmonization of the restrictive and the inclusive texts and labels one office configuration as the norm. The categories teaching-pastor office and mixed adult assemblies are not themselves lexemes (dictionary word-forms) in the cited texts, so the stem imports a polity (church-government) framework the words do not supply. The verdict is derived on the original stem, and the audit records that direct queries confirm the lexicon furnishes neither a settled sense for the hapax (a word that occurs only once in the entire Bible) "to exercise authority" (authenteo) nor a term that fixes the scope of "to teach" (didaskein) or "to keep silent" (sigao).

lay_summary: The question asks whether the Bible reserves the elder and overseer office, and the teaching role over mixed adult gatherings, to qualified men. The Greek words in the cited verses point in two directions, and that is the heart of the dispute. Some verses sound restrictive. First Timothy 2:12 says I do not permit a woman to teach, "to teach" (didaskein), or to "exercise authority" (authentein) over a man. A direct search of the text confirms the verb "to exercise authority" or "to domineer" (authenteo) appears only here in the whole New Testament (a hapax, a word that occurs only once in the entire Bible), so there is no other passage to fix its sense, and the lexicon lists it with two meanings at once, to hold authority over and to domineer. The word "I do not permit" (epitrepo) is in the present tense (an ongoing, simple statement of fact) and is the same verb used elsewhere for letting someone speak on a given occasion, so readers differ on whether it states a permanent rule or a situational one. First Corinthians 14:34 says the women should "keep silent" (sigao) in the assemblies, and the same word is used twice nearby, in verses 28 and 30, for a tongue-speaker and a prophet who should fall silent in specific cases, which raises the question whether the women command is absolute or aimed at a particular disorder. The office lists in 1 Timothy 3:2 and Titus 1:6 say the overseer should be a "one-woman man" (mias gynaikos andra), which on its face pictures a married man, though some read this as a faithfulness standard rather than a rule barring women. Other verses point the opposite way. Galatians 3:28 says there is no male and female, you are all one in Christ, though its argument is about standing and inheritance. Romans 16:1 calls Phoebe a "servant/minister" (diakonos) of her church, a term that ranges from general service to a recognized role. Romans 16:7 greets Junia as notable among the apostles, and the lexical data carries her name in both a feminine and a masculine form, so even the sex of the person is unsettled, and the Greek phrase can mean among the apostles or well known to the apostles. The trouble is that the words themselves do not settle these questions. A single rare verb with two attested senses, a silence command that may be situational, an office phrase that may describe character, and a name that may or may not be feminine all leave room for more than one careful reading. Because the same vocabulary supports both a restrictive and an inclusive conclusion, and because the silence text also carries a known manuscript question about where it belongs, the lexical pattern here is genuinely contested rather than decisive.
